newsitem.title: FRANCE: French far-right shows gains but future limited.
newsitem.headline: French far-right shows gains but future limited.

text.p: The far-right National Front showed considerable new muscle in France's parliamentary election but will remain on the political sidelines so long as the bombastic Jean-Marie Le Pen remains its leader, analysts said on Monday.
They said the xenophobic party had played a key role in turning the French centre-right out of power in Sunday's election and ushering in a leftist alliance.
But they said Le Pen's decision to shun alliances with mainstream parties and bar any shift to the political centre would prevent it from wielding real power in France.

"The National Front has consolidated its position, but it won only one deputy. The problem is that it is alone. Without allies, it cannot have more seats," said Romain Pache, political director of the BVA polling.

Toulon mayor Jean-Marie Le Chevallier won the Front's one seat while Front officials Bruno Megret and Bruno Gollnisch, who have been vying to succeed the 68-year-old Le Pen should he step down, both lost. Le Pen himself did not stand.
Megret and Gollnisch have both hinted the party should move towards the centre to enhance its national political profile.
Megret said on Monday the election showed the main rightist parties, the centrist UDF and the Gaullist RPR, were "doomed and discredited. They failed miserably."

"New parties must emerge, and one of them must accept the National Front as its partner," Megret told France Inter radio. "We agree to an alliance with the partners that are bound to emerge from the smouldering ruins."

But Le Pen showed his contempt for the mainstream in the campaign's final days, throwing a female Socialist candidate to the ground, shouting obscenities at anti-Front protesters and displaying the "head" of a second female Socialist candidate -- actually a photograph -- on a platter at a campaign rally.
"Le Pen has chosen another path. His tactics hurt him. The 'head on a platter' shows his refusal to move to the centre and his desire to remain outside the mainstream," Pache told Reuters.
The Front nonetheless outdid itself in the two-round parliamentary election.

Its first-round score of 14.94 percent, up from 12.41 percent in 1993 legislative elections and just a shade below Le Pen's 15 percent in the 1995 presidential election, gave it candidates in 132 of 577 constituencies in Sunday's runoff.

In the second-round vote, unprecedented numbers of Front voters, heeding Le Pen's advice, backed leftist candidates in order to help "zap the right" from power. The shift was particularly striking among working-class people, previously little drawn to the extreme-right, analysts said.

Le Pen had argued that a leftist win, requiring Socialist leader Lionel Jospin to share power as premier with Gaullist President Jacques Chirac, would lead to gridlock and new parliamentary or presidential elections offering the Front yet another chance.

Of the 76 constituencies in which a National Front candidate competed in a three-way runoff, the Front split the rightist vote and enabled the left to win 47 seats to 29 for the right, according to the French daily le Monde.
"The Front has become a party that can now prevent the right from winning an election. This gives it a very important role," said Pache.

The results also show that the Front has become a real rival to the Socialists for the working-class vote, said Pierre Giacometti of the IPSOS polling firm, adding that the party's appeal to workers went beyond Le Pen.
